processing: Orthodox black tea, plucked as two leaves and a bud and fully oxidised. The estate also makes green tea.
harvest_season: Sold by flush, with spring and autumn lots the ones most often named by retailers.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark leaf with golden tips in the higher SFTGFOP grades.
appearance_liquor: Clear amber to light copper, as is usual for high-grown Nepali orthodox black tea.
appearance_wet: Mixed coppery and olive-brown leaf, as is usual for a Himalayan orthodox tea.
taste_profile: Muscatel is the note most associated with the garden, in a fragrant, medium-bodied cup, with flush making a clear difference.

brewing.notes: A general starting point for Himalayan orthodox tea. Use cooler water for spring lots, which turn sharp when overheated.

vintage_note: Sold by flush and year: spring and autumn lots from the current harvest are the usual offers, with grades such as SFTGFOP. Like Darjeeling, it is best drunk fresh, within a year or two, so check the year and the flush on the label.
description:
Guranse is a garden in the Dhankuta hills of eastern Nepal, near Hile, and one of the district's three best-known names. Its fields run across a wide span of altitude, from about 1,000 to 2,200 metres, on some 290 hectares.

It makes orthodox tea from two leaves and a bud, in several grades from SFTGFOP tippy leaf to fannings, and also a green tea. The garden is organic-certified.

Muscatel is the note it is known for. Treat it like Darjeeling: cooler water and a careful steep for spring lots, slightly more heat for autumn ones.

Buying is a matter of flush and grade, both usually stated. Comparing a spring and an autumn lot from the same year is a good lesson in what a season does.
history:
The Vaidya family, industrialists, set up the estate in 1999 as a subsidiary of their investment company VOITH. Organic certification is given by one retailer as dating from 2001.

Guranse has worked with more than six hundred local farmers and ran training for growers. Together with other hill farmers, it formed the producers' group HOTPA, which helped develop collective brands for Nepali orthodox tea.
